content: Your doctor has prescribed ranitidine hydrochloride to reduce the production of acid in your stomach. This medication may be administered by adding it to an intravenous (IV) fluid, which will be delivered through a needle or catheter placed in your vein over a period of 15 to 20 minutes, one to four times a day. Alternatively, it may be included in your total parenteral nutrition (TPN) solution. Ranitidine works by decreasing stomach acid to treat or prevent ulcers. It can also alleviate symptoms caused by ulcers, such as stomach pain, diarrhea, and loss of appetite. In some cases, ranitidine may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider (doctor, nurse, or pharmacist) may monitor the effectiveness of your treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well you respond to the medication. Precautions Before receiving ranitidine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to ranitidine or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially acetaminophen (Tylenol), anticoagulants (blood thinners) like warfarin (Coumadin), propantheline, and any vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease or acute porphyria. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking ranitidine, contact your doctor immediately. Administering Your Medication Before administering ranitidine, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or examine the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to ensure your therapy continues without interruption. Side Effects Ranitidine may cause side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: Headache Dizziness Constipation Diarrhea Stomach pain Upset stomach Storing Your Medication Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of ranitidine at a time. If you are receiving ranitidine intravenously, you may be instructed to store it in the refrigerator or freezer. Take your next dose out of the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are directed to store additional ranitidine in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day for the next day’s use. Do not refreeze medications. If you are receiving ranitidine mixed with TPN, you may be instructed to store it in a clean, dry area away from heat. Always store your medication as directed and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will explain how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In Case of Emergency/Overdose If you suspect an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Signs of Infection If you are receiving ranitidine through a vein or under your skin, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection (an infection at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin).
